variants.name: Scala 3 opaque type with extension methods
variants.idiom_name: opaque type Orders = Vector[Order] + extension methods
variants.implementation_notes: In Scala 3 the collection is an opaque type alias inside an object: `opaque type Orders = Vector[Order]`, with the operations as extension methods. Outside the defining scope the alias is abstract, so callers cannot reach the Vector or call its structural methods, while inside the object the invariants are written with ordinary Vector code; there is no wrapper class, no allocation and no boxing overhead. Visibility is per-scope, not per-value: keep the alias inside an object - a top-level opaque alias is transparent in the whole source file - and require callers to import the object to bring the extension methods into scope.
pitfalls: An opaque alias is transparent inside its defining scope, and a top-level alias is transparent in the whole source file; keep it inside the object and publish extension methods only.

The abstraction is not a runtime boundary: outside the scope a cast (asInstanceOf[Vector[Order]]) still reaches the representation, so the sanctioned API must be complete enough that nobody needs one.
Operations that return the underlying Vector (map, ++, sorted used without wrapping) silently drop the type; provide mapping helpers that re-wrap.
Extension methods exist only where imported; a missing import looks like a missing method rather than a domain error.

variants.name: Scala 2.13 IndexedSeq subclass over a private Vector
variants.idiom_name: final class Orders private (xs: Vector[Order]) extends IndexedSeq[Order]
variants.implementation_notes: The pre-Scala-3 realization: a final class with a private primary constructor extending IndexedSeq[Order] over a private Vector. Implementing apply and length satisfies the abstract members and the collections framework supplies the rest of the Seq API (map, filter, mkString, pattern matching as a Seq, use wherever Seq[Order] is expected). Invariants live in the private constructor and in the returning methods, so no caller can inject an unvalidated Vector. Choose it when the codebase is still on Scala 2.13 or when the collection must be a first-class Seq for library interoperability; the Scala 3 opaque type is less code and has no runtime wrapper.
pitfalls: Extending a collection trait means every transformation (map, filter, sorted, ++) returns a plain IndexedSeq/Vector, not Orders; re-wrap in the domain methods where the invariant must survive.
apply must honour the Seq contract (index within [0, length)), or pattern matching, head/tail and every inherited method misbehave.
The private constructor stops unvalidated construction, but code that pattern-matches or calls generic Seq operations receives plain Seqs - the type identity stops at the class boundary.
